title: Form and Table Accessibility
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of form and table accessibility in a browser document.
Apply at least one relevant rule from this lesson to a small HTML example.
Check the result using browser inspection, a validator, or an accessibility checklist.

content.intro: This lesson turns “Form and Table Accessibility” into a practical authoring skill. You will work with associating labels and controls, understand the choices that matter, and check the result instead of relying on guesswork.
content.why_it_matters: Meaningful structure and metadata make content easier to navigate, understand, share, and maintain across different devices and assistive technologies.

content_blocks.title: Form and Table Accessibility concept map
content_blocks.alt_text: A concept map for Form and Table Accessibility, connecting the core idea, key concepts, a relevant example, and a verification step.
content_blocks.caption: Use the example and expected result to check your understanding of Form and Table Accessibility.

content_blocks.title: Why this matters
content_blocks.text: Meaningful structure and metadata make content easier to navigate, understand, share, and maintain across different devices and assistive technologies.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Associate each control with a persistent label. With an explicit label, the label’s for value must exactly match the control’s id.

items.title: Associating labels and controls
items.text: Associate each control with a persistent label. With an explicit label, the label’s for value must exactly match the control’s id.

items.title: Grouping related fields
items.text: Grouping related fields is one of the decisions covered by Form and Table Accessibility. Decide what the markup is meant to communicate, choose the native HTML structure that expresses that meaning, and verify the result in a browser or a relevant validation checklist. Avoid using an element or attribute just because its default appearance seems convenient.

items.title: Providing instructions and error feedback
items.text: Use a repeatable loop: reproduce the issue, inspect the source and rendered DOM, read validator or console output, fix one cause, then retest the expected behavior.

items.title: Structuring data-table headers
items.text: The headers attribute: associates a data cell with one or more header-cell IDs in complex tables.

items.title: Avoiding tables for visual layout
items.text: Avoiding tables for visual layout is one of the decisions covered by Form and Table Accessibility. Decide what the markup is meant to communicate, choose the native HTML structure that expresses that meaning, and verify the result in a browser or a relevant validation checklist. Avoid using an element or attribute just because its default appearance seems convenient.

items.title: Testing complex forms and tables
items.text: Form controls need meaningful labels and names, clear instructions, and constraints that match the data. Treat browser validation as feedback for users, not proof that submitted data is trustworthy.

content_blocks.title: Keep in mind
content_blocks.text: Prefer the native semantic element that communicates intent. Do not choose markup solely for its default visual style.

content.task: Test a short page without relying on color alone: navigate with the keyboard, inspect headings/labels, and write down one improvement.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use the relevant concept from Form and Table Accessibility.
Keep IDs unique and use valid nesting.
Check the result in a browser and record one finding.
hints: Start with the smallest valid example for form and table accessibility.
Add one element or attribute at a time, then check the result.
Compare the source and rendered DOM if the behavior surprises you.
content.expected_output: A caption names the table. Header cells identify each column and each row.

troubleshooting.symptom: The expected content does not appear.
troubleshooting.check: Confirm the file was saved with an .html extension and inspect its path and nesting.
Check the resolved URL and confirm the referenced file or external resource exists and allows the request.

troubleshooting.symptom: The page looks correct but the markup may be invalid.
troubleshooting.check: Run the Nu Html Checker and follow its first relevant diagnostic, then validate again.

common_mistakes.why: The default appearance is not the element’s main meaning and can make navigation or maintenance harder.
common_mistakes.fix: Choose the element that matches the content purpose, then use CSS for presentation.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a browser’s recovery means the source is valid
common_mistakes.why: Browsers often recover from malformed markup, which can hide defects and produce unexpected document structure.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the rendered DOM and run a validator against the original source.

common_mistakes.why: Missing files, narrow viewports, keyboard access, invalid input, or other states can expose defects.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected state plus one realistic edge case and an accessibility path.

summary: Form and Table Accessibility is about expressing document structure or behavior intentionally.
Form controls need meaningful labels and names, clear instructions, and constraints that match the data. Treat browser validation as feedback for users, not proof that submitted data is trustworthy.
Verify both markup and behavior; do not infer correctness from appearance alone.
